ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / Skógafoss → Reynisfjara / ✈️ The DC-3 Wreck
en: On **21 November 1973** it was flying from **Höfn to Keflavík** when **ice choked both carburettors over the Vatnajökull ice cap** and both engines quit. The tourist story that it "ran out of fuel" is false — it iced up and became, in the co-pilot's words, "a massively overweight glider."

ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / Skógafoss → Reynisfjara / ✈️ The DC-3 Wreck
en: The pilot turned **south for the coast** and put it down on the black sand. **All seven crew walked away.** The Navy stripped the useful parts and left the shell.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / Skógafoss → Reynisfjara / 🚪 Dýrhólaey
en: **Dýrhólaey** was born underwater ~**100,000 years ago** in a submarine eruption — half tuff (**Háey**), half basalt (**Lágey**) — then hammered by waves into a huge natural **sea arch**. In **October 1993** a pilot flew a small plane clean through it **three times** (once could've been luck).

ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / Skógafoss → Reynisfjara / 🚪 Dýrhólaey
en: On top sits a **castle-like lighthouse** — Iceland's **first landfall light and brightest**, seen **43 km** out to sea; the current 1927 tower was designed by state architect **Guðjón Samúelsson** (yes — the same man behind that little church back down the road, and Hallgrímskirkja).

ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / Skógafoss → Reynisfjara / 🚪 Dýrhólaey

Parts close in summer for **nesting puffins**: this is a full **seabird city**, a **protected reserve since 1978** under **100 m cliffs** — the birds were here first, and the reserve rules say so.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / Skógafoss → Reynisfjara / 🚪 Dýrhólaey
en: The flyers have names: pilot **Arngrímur Jóhannsson** and MP **Árni Johnsen**, who took a light aircraft through the arch in **October 1993** — three passes, to prove the first wasn't luck.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / Skógafoss → Reynisfjara / 🚪 Dýrhólaey
en: The name is literal: **Dýrhólaey** means **door-hill island** — the hill with the doorway through it. The first light went up here in **1910**; the tower you can see replaced it in 1927.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / Skógafoss → Reynisfjara / 🚪 Dýrhólaey

ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / Reynisfjara → Vík / 🌋 Katla
en: Under that ice sits **Katla**: a **caldera ~10 km across**, summit **1,512 m**, hidden beneath **Mýrdalsjökull** — **520 km² of ice as measured in 2019**, down from about **607 km² around the year 2000** and **736 km² at its Little Ice Age peak around 1890.** Being subglacial is the whole danger — she doesn't just throw ash, she **flash-melts the glacier into floods.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / Reynisfjara → Vík / 🌋 Katla
en: She's erupted **at least 21 times in the last 1,100 years**, with gaps running from **about 13 years to about 80, averaging just under 50** — usually bigger than her famous neighbour Eyjafjallajökull's 2010 show. The last eruption up through the ice — **1918** — lasted **24 days** and dumped **about 200 million m³ (0.2 km³) of sand**, pushing **the shore south of Hjörleifshöfði out by more than 3 km.** The volcano literally added land.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / Reynisfjara → Vík / 🌋 Katla
en: It is now **108 years since 1918 — the longest quiet spell on her record.** She even leaks CO₂ while dormant — one study put her among **Earth's biggest volcanic CO₂ sources.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / Reynisfjara → Vík / 🌋 Katla
en: Her system also produced **Eldgjá**, which began in the **spring of 939 CE** and ran on, at least episodically, into the **autumn of 940** — one of the largest lava floods of the last 2,000 years. When this family goes big, it goes very big.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / Reynisfjara → Vík / 🌋 Katla
en: An eruption under ice makes a **jökulhlaup** — a glacial flood that can push **up to ~300,000 m³ a second** to the sea, faster than a galloping horse. The town ahead, **Vík**, has been drilling for this for decades.

en: **Hjörleifshöfði** is a **221 m móberg cape** named after **Hjörleifur**, the **blood-brother** of Iceland's first settler **Ingólfur Arnarson.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🛡️ Hjörleifshöfði
en: Around **875 CE** Hjörleifur forced his enslaved Irishmen to **drag his plough** like oxen; they killed his one ox, **blamed a bear** — and it worked, because Iceland *has no bears* and the newcomers didn't know that yet. When the men scattered to hunt the imaginary bear, the thralls murdered them and fled to the islands offshore. Ingólfur tracked them down and killed them; those islands are the **Vestmannaeyjar**, the "Isles of the West Men," named for the very Irishmen who did the deed.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🛡️ Hjörleifshöfði
en: At its base sits **Kötluklettur**, "Katla's Rock." The tale: **Katla**, a housekeeper at nearby **Þykkvabæjarklaustur** with **magic breeches** that made her run impossibly fast, killed the shepherd boy **Barði** for borrowing them, hid him in a **vat of skyr** — then, as the skyr ran low and discovery loomed, threw herself into the glacier. Every eruption, they say, is her ghost. **The volcano is named after her.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Ölfusá
en: Only **~25 km long**, yet **Iceland's largest river by discharge** — about **400 m³ every second** off a **~5,760 km² basin**. Not the longest; just the one you absolutely could not cross.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Ölfusá
en: It follows the **South Iceland Seismic Zone**, zig-zagging along fault lines. Beside it lies **Þjórsárhraun** — about **8,700 years** old, roughly **1,000 km²**, the **longest lava flow in Iceland**. Vísindavefur puts it higher than that (id=87471, Haraldur Sigurðsson, January 2025): *“Þjórsárhraun er stærsta hraun sem runnið hefur á jörðinni síðan ísöldinni lauk”* — the largest lava flow to have run anywhere on Earth since the Ice Age ended.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Ölfusá
en: For centuries the **ultimate obstacle**: unfordable, no bridge, just a ferry at **Laugardælir** paid in **cattle or cod** to reach the harbour at **Eyrarbakki**. When it flooded catastrophically in **1623**, a bishop blamed a giant river serpent — an “ice worm.” (It was an **ice-jam flood**; the serpent just got the better press.)

ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Ölfusá
en: That lava has a proper name and a frankly silly scale: **Þjórsárhraunið mikla**, the Great Þjórsá Lava. It erupted **about 8,700 years ago** from a **fissure 20 to 30 km long** in the **Veiðivötn swarm of the Bárðarbunga system**, well up in the interior, then ran **about 130 km to the sea**, reaching the coast **between the Þjórsá and the Ölfusá.** Total volume: **25 cubic kilometres.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Ölfusá
en: On the magnitude scale Vísindavefur rates it **MS-9 — the largest Icelandic eruption by volume of erupted material** — ahead of **Eldgjá at MS-8** and a long way ahead of **Laki 1783 at MS-6.5.** That scale is logarithmic, so the gaps are wider than they look. Keep one distinction straight, though: largest by volume is not the same as **most powerful**, and that title goes to **Eldgjá**. The same system gave us **Vatnaöldur in 871** and **Veiðivötn in 1477.** (The biggest eruption this island ever produced is shaped like a field. You cannot see it, and that is exactly how large it is.)

ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Hveragerði
en: Veðurstofa Íslands logged it to the minute — **fimmtudaginn 29. maí kl. 15:45**, **2008** — epicentre at **Ingólfsfjall in Ölfus, about 5 km north-west of Selfoss**, with a very large number of aftershocks behind it. It was a **doublet**: **Mw 5.8 beneath Ingólfsfjall** set off **Mw 5.9 on the Kross fault about 5 km to the west** **within 3 seconds**, for a **composite Mw 6.1**. (Moment adds, magnitude doesn't — 5.8 plus 5.9 comes out at Mw 6.06. The **6.3** you will still see quoted was the figure announced in Iceland that same day, a teleseismic estimate.) It shook the town at up to **~0.88 g** (near 1 g: the earth shoving as hard as gravity), split buildings and re-plumbed the hot springs. (Two quakes, one bang; nobody in town stopped to count.)

ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Hveragerði
en: Cheap volcanic heat made it a **greenhouse town** from the 1920s (Iceland's **first geothermally heated greenhouse** went up in **Mosfellssveit in 1924**) and Iceland's **market garden**: tomatoes, cucumbers, flowers — and, at the horticultural college, **experimental bananas** planted ~**1950**: about **a tonne a year, never commercial**. Iceland is *not* a banana republic — just the most over-hyped tonne of fruit in Europe.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Hveragerði
en: For scale: **about 140 people at the end of 1941**, **about 400 by 1946** — the year the district was formally constituted — and **about 3,350 today, 3,344 at the start of 2026** (Hagstofa MAN02005; the town passed 3,000 in 2023). The name is far older than the town. **Hveragerði first appears in Fitjaannáll shortly before 1700**, in an account of an erupting hot spring that **shifted position during earthquakes in 1597**, and by the description of Ölfus written in **1703** the springs were already in daily use for **bathing, boiling and washing.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Hveragerði
en: Rather than hide it, the town put it on display — and the best thing in **Sunnumörk** was never meant to be an exhibit at all: when the centre was under construction in **2003** an **earthquake fissure was found in the ground beneath it**, and instead of filling it in they **lit it and left it on show.** That became **Skjálftinn 2008**, “The Quake” — stand on the crack, then ride the shaking simulator, which runs at **over 6 on the Richter scale.** **Admission is free**; you pay only if you want a turn in the simulator.
